title: R for Microeconometrics
text:
Preface
These notes show how to estimate the standard microeconometric models in R. Each chapter gives a short description of the model, the R code, and the output, with a few comments on how to read it. The notes accompany the Microeconometrics course at LMU Munich. They do not replace a textbook; for the theory see the references at the end.

title: R for Microeconometrics
text:
Setup
Install the packages once:
install.packages(c("wooldridge", "car", "lmtest", "DescTools", "mlogit", "rms",
                   "pastecs", "MASS", "pscl", "VGAM", "censReg", "survival",
                   "haven", "sampleSelection"))
Most data sets come with the R packages wooldridge (Wooldridge 2020) and mlogit (Croissant 2020). The Heckman example in Chapter 5 uses mus16data.dta from Cameron and Trivedi (2010), which is not included here. Download it from the book’s website and save it in your working directory.
The same code is also available as plain R scripts in the GitHub repository.




Cameron, A. Colin, and Pravin K. Trivedi. 2010. Microeconometrics Using Stata, Revised Edition. College Station, TX: Stata Press.


Croissant, Yves. 2020. “Estimation of Random Utility Models in R: The mlogit Package.” Journal of Statistical Software 95 (11): 1–41.


Wooldridge, Jeffrey M. 2020. Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach. 7th ed. Boston: Cengage.

title: 1  Binary Response Models
text:
1.1 Example: Labor force participation of married women
The outcome \(y\) takes the values 0 and 1, and we model the response probability \[
P(y = 1 \mid x) = G(x\beta).
\] The three standard choices for \(G\) are
Logit and probit are estimated by maximum likelihood. Their fitted probabilities always lie between 0 and 1; the LPM’s need not.
The data set mroz contains 753 married women. The outcome inlf equals 1 if the woman was in the labor force in 1975. Regressors are other household income (nwifeinc, in $1000), years of education, experience and its square, age, and the number of children younger than 6 and between 6 and 18.
data(mroz, package = "wooldridge")
library(car); library(lmtest)

title: 1  Binary Response Models
text:
1.1.1 Linear probability model
In the LPM the error is heteroskedastic by construction, since \(\text{Var}(y \mid x) = x\beta(1-x\beta)\). We therefore use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (vcov = hccm).

linprob <- lm(inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + kidsge6,
              data = mroz)
coeftest(linprob, vcov = hccm)

#> 
#> t test of coefficients:
#> 
#>                Estimate  Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  0.58551922  0.15358032  3.8125  0.000149 ***
#> nwifeinc    -0.00340517  0.00155826 -2.1852  0.029182 *  
#> educ         0.03799530  0.00733982  5.1766 2.909e-07 ***
#> exper        0.03949239  0.00598359  6.6001 7.800e-11 ***
#> I(exper^2)  -0.00059631  0.00019895 -2.9973  0.002814 ** 
#> age         -0.01609081  0.00241459 -6.6640 5.183e-11 ***
#> kidslt6     -0.26181047  0.03215160 -8.1430 1.621e-15 ***
#> kidsge6      0.01301223  0.01366031  0.9526  0.341123    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Each coefficient is the change in the participation probability for a one-unit change in the regressor. For example, one more young child lowers the probability by about 26 percentage points, holding the other variables fixed.


1.1.2 Logit

logitres <- glm(inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + kidsge6,
                family = binomial(link = logit), data = mroz)
summary(logitres)

#> 
#> Call:
#> glm(formula = inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + 
#>     kidslt6 + kidsge6, family = binomial(link = logit), data = mroz)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  0.425452   0.860365   0.495  0.62095    
#> nwifeinc    -0.021345   0.008421  -2.535  0.01126 *  
#> educ         0.221170   0.043439   5.091 3.55e-07 ***
#> exper        0.205870   0.032057   6.422 1.34e-10 ***
#> I(exper^2)  -0.003154   0.001016  -3.104  0.00191 ** 
#> age         -0.088024   0.014573  -6.040 1.54e-09 ***
#> kidslt6     -1.443354   0.203583  -7.090 1.34e-12 ***
#> kidsge6      0.060112   0.074789   0.804  0.42154    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
#> 
#>     Null deviance: 1029.75  on 752  degrees of freedom
#> Residual deviance:  803.53  on 745  degrees of freedom
#> AIC: 819.53
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

logLik(logitres)

#> 'log Lik.' -401.7652 (df=8)


The logit coefficients are not partial effects on the probability; only their signs and relative sizes can be read directly. A common transformation is the odds ratio \(\exp(\beta_j)\): the factor by which the odds \(P/(1-P)\) change when \(x_j\) increases by one unit.

exp(coef(logitres))

#> (Intercept)    nwifeinc        educ       exper  I(exper^2)         age 
#>   1.5302825   0.9788810   1.2475360   1.2285929   0.9968509   0.9157386 
#>     kidslt6     kidsge6 
#>   0.2361344   1.0619557


Pseudo \(R^2\). McFadden’s measure is \(1 - \ell_{ur}/\ell_0\), where \(\ell_0\) is the log likelihood of a model with only an intercept. For binary outcomes it equals one minus the ratio of the residual to the null deviance. DescTools reports several other versions.

1 - logitres$deviance / logitres$null.deviance

#> [1] 0.2196814

library(DescTools)
PseudoR2(logitres, which = "all")

#>        McFadden     McFaddenAdj        CoxSnell      Nagelkerke   AldrichNelson 
#>       0.2196814       0.2041436       0.2594927       0.3481893       0.2310176 
#> VeallZimmermann           Efron McKelveyZavoina            Tjur             AIC 
#>       0.3999487       0.2682411       0.3645020       0.2701512     819.5303023 
#>             BIC          logLik         logLik0              G2 
#>     856.5228241    -401.7651511    -514.8732046     226.2161069




1.1.3 Probit

probitres <- glm(inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + kidsge6,
                 family = binomial(link = probit), data = mroz)
summary(probitres)

#> 
#> Call:
#> glm(formula = inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + 
#>     kidslt6 + kidsge6, family = binomial(link = probit), data = mroz)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  0.2700736  0.5080782   0.532  0.59503    
#> nwifeinc    -0.0120236  0.0049392  -2.434  0.01492 *  
#> educ         0.1309040  0.0253987   5.154 2.55e-07 ***
#> exper        0.1233472  0.0187587   6.575 4.85e-11 ***
#> I(exper^2)  -0.0018871  0.0005999  -3.145  0.00166 ** 
#> age         -0.0528524  0.0084624  -6.246 4.22e-10 ***
#> kidslt6     -0.8683247  0.1183773  -7.335 2.21e-13 ***
#> kidsge6      0.0360056  0.0440303   0.818  0.41350    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
#> 
#>     Null deviance: 1029.7  on 752  degrees of freedom
#> Residual deviance:  802.6  on 745  degrees of freedom
#> AIC: 818.6
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

logLik(probitres)

#> 'log Lik.' -401.3022 (df=8)

1 - probitres$deviance / probitres$null.deviance

#> [1] 0.2205805


Logit coefficients are roughly 1.6 times the probit coefficients because the logistic distribution has a larger variance. The two models usually give very similar probabilities and partial effects.


1.1.4 Likelihood ratio tests
The LR statistic is \(LR = 2(\ell_{ur} - \ell_r)\), which is asymptotically \(\chi^2_q\) under \(H_0\), with \(q\) the number of restrictions. For the test that all slope coefficients are zero, \(\ell_r = \ell_0\) and the statistic equals the null deviance minus the residual deviance.

probitres$null.deviance - probitres$deviance

#> [1] 227.142

lrtest(probitres)

#> Likelihood ratio test
#> 
#> Model 1: inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + 
#>     kidsge6
#> Model 2: inlf ~ 1
#>   #Df  LogLik Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)    
#> 1   8 -401.30                         
#> 2   1 -514.87 -7 227.14  < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Next we test \(H_0\): experience and age do not matter (\(q = 3\), since experience enters with its square).

restr <- glm(inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + kidslt6 + kidsge6,
             family = binomial(link = probit), data = mroz)
lrtest(restr, probitres)

#> Likelihood ratio test
#> 
#> Model 1: inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + kidslt6 + kidsge6
#> Model 2: inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + 
#>     kidsge6
#>   #Df  LogLik Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)    
#> 1   5 -464.82                         
#> 2   8 -401.30  3 127.03  < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




1.1.5 Predicted probabilities
With type = "response", predict() returns probabilities. Consider two “extreme” women: the first has low education, no experience, is 20 years old and has two young children; the second has 17 years of education, 30 years of experience, is 52 and has no children.

xpred <- list(nwifeinc = c(100, 0), educ = c(5, 17), exper = c(0, 30),
              age = c(20, 52), kidslt6 = c(2, 0), kidsge6 = c(0, 0))
rbind(LPM    = predict(linprob,   xpred, type = "response"),
      logit  = predict(logitres,  xpred, type = "response"),
      probit = predict(probitres, xpred, type = "response"))

#>                   1         2
#> LPM    -0.410458206 1.0428084
#> logit   0.005218002 0.9500491
#> probit  0.001065043 0.9598690


The LPM predicts probabilities of -0.41 and 1.04, outside the unit interval. Logit and probit predictions stay between 0 and 1.


1.1.6 Average partial effects
For a continuous regressor, the partial effect in logit and probit is \[
\frac{\partial P(y=1 \mid x)}{\partial x_j} = g(x\beta)\,\beta_j,
\] where \(g\) is the density (\(\phi\) for probit, \(\lambda\) for logit). It depends on \(x\). The average partial effect (APE) averages it over the sample: \(\widehat{APE}_j = \hat\beta_j \cdot n^{-1}\sum_i g(x_i\hat\beta)\). These APEs are comparable to the LPM coefficients.

xb.log  <- predict(logitres)    # linear index x'b
xb.prob <- predict(probitres)

factor.log  <- mean(dlogis(xb.log))
factor.prob <- mean(dnorm(xb.prob))
cbind(factor.log, factor.prob)

#>      factor.log factor.prob
#> [1,]  0.1785796   0.3007555

APE.lin  <- coef(linprob) * 1
APE.log  <- coef(logitres) * factor.log
APE.prob <- coef(probitres) * factor.prob
round(cbind(APE.lin, APE.log, APE.prob), 4)

#>             APE.lin APE.log APE.prob
#> (Intercept)  0.5855  0.0760   0.0812
#> nwifeinc    -0.0034 -0.0038  -0.0036
#> educ         0.0380  0.0395   0.0394
#> exper        0.0395  0.0368   0.0371
#> I(exper^2)  -0.0006 -0.0006  -0.0006
#> age         -0.0161 -0.0157  -0.0159
#> kidslt6     -0.2618 -0.2578  -0.2612
#> kidsge6      0.0130  0.0107   0.0108


Ignore the row for the intercept. Note that for exper, which enters with a square, the formula \(\hat\beta_j \cdot \text{factor}\) is not the APE of experience; the APE then needs the derivative of the whole index. The same holds for discrete regressors such as kidslt6, where the exact APE is the average difference in predicted probabilities. The simple scale factor gives a good approximation in practice.


1.1.7 The three models in a picture
To see how the three models fit, we simulate data from a probit model: \(y = 1\) if \(1 + 3x + e > 2\), with \(x, e \sim N(0,1)\).

set.seed(28052020)
x <- rnorm(1000, 0, 1)
e <- rnorm(1000, 0, 1)
y <- ifelse(1 + 3*x + e > 2, 1, 0)

linear <- lm(y ~ x)
logit  <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = logit))
probit <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = probit))

xp <- seq(from = min(x), to = max(x), length = 1000)
plot(x, y)
lines(xp, predict(linear, list(x = xp), type = "response"), col = 2, lwd = 1)
lines(xp, predict(logit,  list(x = xp), type = "response"), col = 3, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(xp, predict(probit, list(x = xp), type = "response"), col = 4, lwd = 1)
legend("topleft", c("LPM", "Logit", "Probit"), col = 2:4, lwd = c(1, 2, 1), lty = c(1, 2, 1))







Figure 1.1: Fitted probabilities of the LPM, logit and probit for simulated data.





The logit and probit curves are almost identical. The LPM line goes below 0 and above 1 at the ends.

title: 1  Binary Response Models
text:
1.2 Second example: Smoking during pregnancy
The data set bwght contains 1388 births. We define smoke = 1 if the mother smoked during pregnancy and relate it to the mother’s education, race and log family income. The steps are the same as above.

data(bwght, package = "wooldridge")
bwght$smoke <- ifelse(bwght$cigs > 0, 1, 0)

linprob2   <- lm(smoke ~ motheduc + white + log(faminc), data = bwght)
logitres2  <- glm(smoke ~ motheduc + white + log(faminc),
                  family = binomial(link = logit), data = bwght)
probitres2 <- glm(smoke ~ motheduc + white + log(faminc),
                  family = binomial(link = probit), data = bwght)

coeftest(linprob2, vcov = hccm)

#> 
#> t test of coefficients:
#> 
#>               Estimate Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  0.6255033  0.0567344 11.0251 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> motheduc    -0.0293207  0.0041861 -7.0042 3.865e-12 ***
#> white        0.0483640  0.0253627  1.9069  0.056742 .  
#> log(faminc) -0.0427425  0.0133599 -3.1993  0.001409 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

summary(probitres2)

#> 
#> Call:
#> glm(formula = smoke ~ motheduc + white + log(faminc), family = binomial(link = probit), 
#>     data = bwght)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  1.12627    0.25037   4.498 6.85e-06 ***
#> motheduc    -0.14506    0.02070  -7.009 2.40e-12 ***
#> white        0.18968    0.11068   1.714 0.086576 .  
#> log(faminc) -0.16691    0.04984  -3.349 0.000812 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
#> 
#>     Null deviance: 1186.2  on 1386  degrees of freedom
#> Residual deviance: 1093.5  on 1383  degrees of freedom
#>   (1 observation deleted due to missingness)
#> AIC: 1101.5
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


Test of \(H_0\): race does not matter.

restr2 <- glm(smoke ~ motheduc + log(faminc), family = binomial(link = probit),
              data = bwght)
lrtest(restr2, probitres2)

#> Likelihood ratio test
#> 
#> Model 1: smoke ~ motheduc + log(faminc)
#> Model 2: smoke ~ motheduc + white + log(faminc)
#>   #Df  LogLik Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)  
#> 1   3 -548.29                       
#> 2   4 -546.77  1 3.0349    0.08149 .
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Average partial effects:

f.log  <- mean(dlogis(predict(logitres2)))
f.prob <- mean(dnorm(predict(probitres2)))
round(cbind(LPM = coef(linprob2), logit = coef(logitres2) * f.log,
            probit = coef(probitres2) * f.prob), 4)

#>                 LPM   logit  probit
#> (Intercept)  0.6255  0.2424  0.2439
#> motheduc    -0.0293 -0.0303 -0.0314
#> white        0.0484  0.0414  0.0411
#> log(faminc) -0.0427 -0.0357 -0.0361

title: 2  Multinomial Response Models
text:
2.1 Example: Choice of fishing mode
Now the outcome is one of \(J\) unordered alternatives, \(y \in \{1, \dots, J\}\). The models differ in the type of regressors:
All logit models above have the independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) property: the ratio \(P(y=j)/P(y=k)\) does not depend on the other alternatives. Nested logit and multinomial probit relax it.
We use the package mlogit (Croissant 2020). In its formula y ~ z | x | w, the first part holds alternative-specific regressors with a common coefficient, the second part individual-specific regressors, and the third alternative-specific regressors with alternative-specific coefficients. A 0 in the second part removes the alternative-specific intercepts.
The data set Fishing contains the choice of fishing mode (beach, pier, private boat, charter boat) of 1182 anglers (see also Cameron and Trivedi 2005). For each mode we observe its price and catch rate; income is individual-specific. mlogit needs the data in “long” format, with one row per individual and alternative.
data("Fishing", package = "mlogit")
library(mlogit)
table(Fishing$mode)

#> 
#>   beach    pier    boat charter 
#>     134     178     418     452

mFishing <- dfidx(Fishing, choice = "mode", varying = 2:9)
head(mFishing, 4)

#> ~~~~~~~
#>  first 4 observations out of 4728 
#> ~~~~~~~
#>    mode   income  price  catch    idx
#> 1 FALSE 7083.332 157.93 0.0678 1:each
#> 2 FALSE 7083.332 157.93 0.2601 1:boat
#> 3  TRUE 7083.332 182.93 0.5391 1:rter
#> 4 FALSE 7083.332 157.93 0.0503 1:pier
#> 
#> ~~~ indexes ~~~~
#>   id1     id2
#> 1   1   beach
#> 2   1    boat
#> 3   1 charter
#> 4   1    pier
#> indexes:  1, 2

title: 2  Multinomial Response Models
text:
2.1.1 Multinomial logit
Only income, with private boat as the base alternative.

multi <- mlogit(mode ~ 0 | income, mFishing, reflevel = "boat")
summary(multi)

#> 
#> Call:
#> mlogit(formula = mode ~ 0 | income, data = mFishing, reflevel = "boat", 
#>     method = "nr")
#> 
#> Frequencies of alternatives:choice
#>    boat   beach charter    pier 
#> 0.35364 0.11337 0.38240 0.15059 
#> 
#> nr method
#> 4 iterations, 0h:0m:0s 
#> g'(-H)^-1g = 8.32E-07 
#> gradient close to zero 
#> 
#> Coefficients :
#>                        Estimate  Std. Error z-value  Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept):beach   -7.3892e-01  1.9673e-01 -3.7560 0.0001727 ***
#> (Intercept):charter  6.0237e-01  1.3610e-01  4.4261 9.597e-06 ***
#> (Intercept):pier     7.5230e-02  1.8324e-01  0.4106 0.6814005    
#> income:beach        -9.1906e-05  4.0664e-05 -2.2602 0.0238116 *  
#> income:charter      -1.2355e-04  2.7911e-05 -4.4265 9.577e-06 ***
#> income:pier         -2.3531e-04  4.3668e-05 -5.3886 7.101e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-Likelihood: -1477.2
#> McFadden R^2:  0.013736 
#> Likelihood ratio test : chisq = 41.145 (p.value = 6.0931e-09)


Each coefficient refers to the comparison with the base: a positive income coefficient for an alternative means that higher income makes that alternative more likely relative to the private boat.


2.1.2 Conditional logit
Only price and catch rate. The first model includes alternative-specific intercepts, the second does not.

condi <- mlogit(mode ~ catch + price, mFishing)
summary(condi)

#> 
#> Call:
#> mlogit(formula = mode ~ catch + price, data = mFishing, method = "nr")
#> 
#> Frequencies of alternatives:choice
#>   beach    boat charter    pier 
#> 0.11337 0.35364 0.38240 0.15059 
#> 
#> nr method
#> 7 iterations, 0h:0m:0s 
#> g'(-H)^-1g = 6.22E-06 
#> successive function values within tolerance limits 
#> 
#> Coefficients :
#>                       Estimate Std. Error  z-value  Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept):boat     0.8713749  0.1140428   7.6408 2.154e-14 ***
#> (Intercept):charter  1.4988884  0.1329328  11.2755 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> (Intercept):pier     0.3070552  0.1145738   2.6800 0.0073627 ** 
#> catch                0.3771689  0.1099707   3.4297 0.0006042 ***
#> price               -0.0247896  0.0017044 -14.5444 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-Likelihood: -1230.8
#> McFadden R^2:  0.17823 
#> Likelihood ratio test : chisq = 533.88 (p.value = < 2.22e-16)

condix <- mlogit(mode ~ catch + price | 0, mFishing)
summary(condix)

#> 
#> Call:
#> mlogit(formula = mode ~ catch + price | 0, data = mFishing, method = "nr")
#> 
#> Frequencies of alternatives:choice
#>   beach    boat charter    pier 
#> 0.11337 0.35364 0.38240 0.15059 
#> 
#> nr method
#> 6 iterations, 0h:0m:0s 
#> g'(-H)^-1g = 0.000179 
#> successive function values within tolerance limits 
#> 
#> Coefficients :
#>         Estimate Std. Error z-value  Pr(>|z|)    
#> catch  0.9530982  0.0894134  10.659 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> price -0.0204765  0.0012231 -16.742 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-Likelihood: -1312


The coefficients have the expected signs: a higher price lowers, and a higher catch rate raises, the probability of choosing an alternative.


2.1.3 Both types of regressors

mix <- mlogit(mode ~ catch + price | income, mFishing, reflevel = "boat")
summary(mix)

#> 
#> Call:
#> mlogit(formula = mode ~ catch + price | income, data = mFishing, 
#>     reflevel = "boat", method = "nr")
#> 
#> Frequencies of alternatives:choice
#>    boat   beach charter    pier 
#> 0.35364 0.11337 0.38240 0.15059 
#> 
#> nr method
#> 7 iterations, 0h:0m:0s 
#> g'(-H)^-1g = 1.37E-05 
#> successive function values within tolerance limits

section: 2.2 Nested logit: Heating and cooling systems
text:
2.2 Nested logit: Heating and cooling systems
The nested logit groups alternatives into nests. IIA holds within a nest but not across nests. The data set HC contains the choice of heating and cooling system of 250 newly built houses in California (Croissant 2020). There are seven alternatives: four with central cooling (gcc, ecc, erc, hpc) and three without (gc, ec, er). Regressors are installation and operating costs of the heating (ich, och) and cooling (icca, occa) systems, and income. The code follows the example in the mlogit documentation.

data("HC", package = "mlogit")
HC <- dfidx(HC, varying = c(2:8, 10:16), choice = "depvar")
cooling.modes <- idx(HC, 2) %in% c("gcc", "ecc", "erc", "hpc")
room.modes    <- idx(HC, 2) %in% c("erc", "er")

# cooling costs are zero for alternatives without cooling
HC$icca[!cooling.modes] <- 0
HC$occa[!cooling.modes] <- 0

# income for room-system and cooling alternatives, and a cooling intercept
HC$inc.cooling <- HC$inc.room <- 0
HC$inc.cooling[cooling.modes] <- HC$income[cooling.modes]
HC$inc.room[room.modes]       <- HC$income[room.modes]
HC$int.cooling <- as.numeric(cooling.modes)

nested <- mlogit(depvar ~ ich + och + icca + occa + inc.room + inc.cooling + int.cooling | 0,
                 HC, nests = list(cooling = c("gcc", "ecc", "erc", "hpc"),
                                  other   = c("gc", "ec", "er")),
                 un.nest.el = TRUE)
summary(nested)

#> 
#> Call:

title: 3  Ordered Response Models
text:
3.1 Example: Asset allocation in pension plans
When the alternatives have a natural order, we use a latent variable model: \[
y^* = x\beta + e, \qquad y = j \ \text{ if } \ \alpha_{j-1} < y^* \le \alpha_j, \quad j = 0, 1, \dots, J,
\] with cut points \(\alpha_{-1} = -\infty < \alpha_0 < \dots < \alpha_J = \infty\). With \(e \sim N(0,1)\) this is the ordered probit, with a logistic \(e\) the ordered logit. Then \[
P(y = j \mid x) = G(\alpha_j - x\beta) - G(\alpha_{j-1} - x\beta).
\] A positive \(\beta_k\) shifts probability mass to higher categories: it lowers the probability of the lowest and raises the probability of the highest category. For the categories in between, the sign of the effect is not determined by the sign of \(\beta_k\).
The data set pension contains 194 workers and the asset allocation of their pension funds (Wooldridge 2020). The outcome pctstck is 0 (mostly bonds), 50 (mixed) or 100 (mostly stocks).
data(pension, package = "wooldridge")
table(pension$pctstck)

#> 
#>   0  50 100 
#>  64  72  58
Regressors include whether the worker can choose the allocation (choice), gender, race, whether the plan is a profit-sharing plan (prftshr), age, education, wealth in 1989 and dummies for family income classes.
We use orm() from the package rms. Note its sign convention: orm() models \(P(y \ge j \mid x) = G(\alpha_j + x\beta)\), so the reported intercepts are the negative cut points, while the slope coefficients have the usual meaning.
library(rms)
ddist <- datadist("choice", "prftshr", "finc25", "finc35", "finc50", "finc75",
                  "finc100", "finc101", "female", "black", "age", "educ", "wealth89")
options(datadist = "ddist")

title: 4  Count Data Models
text:
4.1 Example: Number of children
Count outcomes take the values \(0, 1, 2, \dots\), often with many zeros. The models below all specify the conditional mean as \[
E(y \mid x) = \exp(x\beta),
\] so that \(100\cdot\beta_j\) is approximately the percentage change in \(E(y \mid x)\) for a one-unit increase in \(x_j\).
The data set fertil2 contains 4361 women in Botswana (Wooldridge 2020). The outcome is the number of children ever born.
data(fertil2, package = "wooldridge")
library(pastecs)
stat.desc(fertil2$children)

                     data = fertil2)
negbinreg1$theta

#> [1] 20686.81


The estimated \(\theta\) is very large (and glm.nb() warns that its iteration limit is reached). There is no overdispersion conditional on the regressors, and the negative binomial model reduces to the Poisson model. Compare the coefficients:

round(cbind(Poisson = coef(poissonreg), NegBin = coef(negbinreg1)), 4)

4.1.3 Hurdle model
We use hurdle() from the package pscl. The output has two parts: the count model for the positive counts and the zero hurdle model (logit for \(y > 0\)).

library(pscl)

                    data = fertil2, dist = "poisson", zero.dist = "binomial", link = "logit")

section: 4.2 Second example: Cigarettes smoked per day
text:
4.2 Second example: Cigarettes smoked per day
The data set smoke contains 807 adults (Wooldridge 2020). The outcome is the number of cigarettes smoked per day; 62 percent smoke none.

data(smoke, package = "wooldridge")
smoke$agesq <- smoke$age^2 / 100
stat.desc(smoke$cigs)

#>      nbr.val     nbr.null       nbr.na          min          max        range 
#>  807.0000000  497.0000000    0.0000000    0.0000000   80.0000000   80.0000000 
#>          sum       median         mean      SE.mean CI.mean.0.95          var

#>      std.dev     coef.var 
#>   13.7215161    1.5796382

hist(smoke$cigs, breaks = 15, col = "blue", main = "Cigarettes per day", xlab = "")








Here the outcome is very overdispersed: the variance is 188, the mean 8.7.

4.2.1 Poisson regression

poissonreg2 <- glm(cigs ~ log(cigpric) + log(income) + restaurn + white + educ + age + agesq,
                   data = smoke, family = poisson)
summary(poissonreg2)

The Poisson model fits the many zeros poorly. predprob() gives the predicted probability of each count for every observation; averaging over the sample gives the predicted distribution, which we can compare with the observed share of zeros.

trial <- predprob(poissonreg2)
round(c(observed = mean(smoke$cigs == 0), Poisson = mean(trial[, 1])), 3)

#> observed  Poisson

barplot(colMeans(trial)[1:41], col = "blue", names.arg = 0:40,
        main = "Average predicted probabilities, Poisson")

title: 5  Censored Regression and Sample Selection
text:
5.1 Tobit model
Many outcomes are zero for a part of the population and continuous and positive for the rest, for example expenditures or hours worked. The Tobit model (Tobin 1958) writes \[
y^* = x\beta + u, \quad u \mid x \sim N(0, \sigma^2), \qquad y = \max(0, y^*).
\] It is estimated by maximum likelihood. The coefficients \(\beta\) are the effects on the latent \(y^*\). The partial effect on the observed outcome is \[
\frac{\partial E(y \mid x)}{\partial x_j} = \beta_j \, \Phi(x\beta/\sigma),
\] which is smaller in absolute value than \(\beta_j\).

title: 5  Censored Regression and Sample Selection
text:
5.1.1 Example: Fringe benefits
The data set fringe contains 616 workers (Wooldridge 2020). The outcome hrbens is hourly fringe benefits in dollars; 6.7 percent of the workers have none.
We use censReg() from the package of the same name. In its output, logSigma is \(\log\sigma\).

data(fringe, package = "wooldridge")
library(censReg)
tobit <- censReg(hrbens ~ exper + age + educ + tenure + married + male + white +
                   nrtheast + nrthcen + south + union, data = fringe)
summary(tobit)

#> 
#> Call:
#> censReg(formula = hrbens ~ exper + age + educ + tenure + married + 
#>     male + white + nrtheast + nrthcen + south + union, data = fringe)

#>            616             41            575              0

#> age         -0.002586   0.004436  -0.583   0.5600

#> tenure       0.028710   0.003724   7.710 1.26e-14 ***

#> male         0.255677   0.055169   4.634 3.58e-06 ***

margEff() gives the partial effects on \(E(y \mid x)\), evaluated at the sample means of the regressors.

margEff(tobit)

#>        exper          age         educ       tenure      married         male 
#>  0.003841153 -0.002444660  0.082168957  0.027141600  0.097144242  0.241710153 
#>        white     nrtheast      nrthcen        south        union 
#>  0.094008820 -0.073593747 -0.046268721 -0.023336998  0.381318769


The same model can be estimated with survreg() from the package survival, where the outcome is declared as left-censored at zero. The coefficients are identical; Log(scale) is \(\log\sigma\).

library(survival)
tobitx <- survreg(Surv(hrbens, hrbens > 0, type = "left") ~ exper + age + educ + tenure +
                    married + male + white + nrtheast + nrthcen + south + union,
                  data = fringe, dist = "gaussian")
summary(tobitx)

#> 
#> Call:

#>                Value Std. Error      z       p

title: 5  Censored Regression and Sample Selection

5.2 Heckman selection model
In the selection model (Heckman 1979), the outcome is observed only for a selected part of the sample: \[
\begin{aligned}
d &= 1[z\gamma + v > 0] && \text{(selection equation)}\\
y &= x\beta + u, \ \text{ observed only if } d = 1 && \text{(outcome equation)}
\end{aligned}
\] with \((u, v)\) jointly normal and \(\text{Corr}(u, v) = \rho\). If \(\rho \ne 0\), OLS on the selected sample is inconsistent, because \[
E(y \mid x, d = 1) = x\beta + \rho\sigma_u \, \lambda(z\gamma),
\] where \(\lambda(\cdot) = \phi(\cdot)/\Phi(\cdot)\) is the inverse Mills ratio. The two-step estimator first estimates \(\gamma\) by probit, then regresses \(y\) on \(x\) and \(\lambda(z\hat\gamma)\) by OLS in the selected sample. The coefficient on \(\lambda\) estimates \(\rho\sigma_u\); its \(t\) test is a test of selection bias.

5.2.1 Example: Ambulatory expenditures
We use the data on ambulatory medical expenditures (ambexp) from Cameron and Trivedi (2010). Expenditures are observed for those with positive spending; the outcome equation is for log expenditures. Save mus16data.dta in your working directory first.

library(haven)
mus16data <- read_dta("mus16data.dta")

mus16data$dy  <- as.numeric(mus16data$ambexp > 0)       # selection indicator
mus16data$lny <- ifelse(mus16data$ambexp > 0, log(mus16data$ambexp), NA)
table(mus16data$dy)

#> 
#>    0    1 
#>  526 2802


Regressors are age, gender, years of education, a dummy for Black or Hispanic (blhisp) and the number of chronic diseases (totchr). We estimate the model with selection() from the package sampleSelection.

library(sampleSelection)
heckman <- selection(dy  ~ age + female + educ + blhisp + totchr,
                     lny ~ age + female + educ + blhisp + totchr,
                     data = mus16data, method = "2step")
summary(heckman)

The coefficient on the inverse Mills ratio (invMillsRatio) is -0.44 and not significant at conventional levels, so these data show no clear evidence of selection bias.
Note that both equations here contain the same regressors. The model is then identified only through the nonlinearity of \(\lambda(\cdot)\), which often makes the two-step estimates imprecise. In applications one should have at least one variable in the selection equation that is excluded from the outcome equation. With method = "ml", selection() estimates the model by maximum likelihood instead.
